questions.question: How do you profile a Java application to find performance bottlenecks?
questions.title: Profiling a Java Application to Find Performance Bottlenecks

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have hands-on experience with profiling tools and a systematic approach to diagnosing performance issues in production or staging environments.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping straight to code optimization without first measuring and identifying the actual bottleneck, or only knowing one tool.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention continuous profiling in production using async-profiler or Pyroscope, and explain how you correlate profiler output with APM traces.

questions.direct_answer: Profile using async-profiler or JFR for CPU/memory flamegraphs, identify hot methods, then correlate with APM traces to pinpoint the root cause before optimizing.

sections.title: The Trap of Optimizing Without Measurement
sections.content:
Most performance work fails because engineers start fixing before finding. They notice a slow endpoint, guess that the database is the bottleneck, add an index or a cache layer, and discover the endpoint is still slow — because the actual bottleneck was JSON serialization eating 40% of CPU time. Profiling flips this by showing exactly where the JVM spends its cycles before any code changes happen.

The two tools worth knowing are **async-profiler** and **Java Flight Recorder (JFR)**. Both are sampling profilers that snapshot thread stacks at regular intervals, building a statistical picture of CPU usage with sub-1% overhead — safe enough for production. The output is a **flamegraph**: a visualization where each frame's width is proportional to the time spent in that method. Wide frames near the top of the stack represent genuine hot spots, not just frequently-called parent functions.

The profiling workflow is a disciplined loop: reproduce realistic load, capture for 30+ seconds, identify the widest frame at the top of the stack, apply a targeted fix, then re-capture to verify the frame narrowed or disappeared. Skipping the re-verification step is how performance regressions slip into production unnoticed. Every optimization claim needs a before-and-after flamegraph to back it up.

sections.title: Why You Need Realistic Load Before the Profiler Matters
sections.content:
Profiling an idle application produces misleading flamegraphs. Under real traffic, thread pools contend, GC fires more frequently, connection pools saturate, and lock contention emerges as `Unsafe.park` frames. None of this appears when a single request flows through an otherwise empty system.

Use a load-testing tool like **Gatling** or **k6** to drive traffic at your production p95 request rate. The goal is not stress-testing to failure — it is recreating the concurrency level where the real bottleneck manifests. If your production service handles 500 requests per second with 20ms average latency, simulate that exact profile before attaching the profiler.

Capture should last at least 30 seconds to catch periodic behaviors like G1 mixed collections, background scheduled tasks, or connection pool recycling that coincide with user traffic. A 5-second capture on a quiet JVM tells you nothing useful about how the service performs at 3 AM when the batch job runs alongside the API traffic.

sections.title: Attaching async-profiler and Decoding the Flamegraph
sections.content:
Async-profiler attaches to a running JVM without requiring a restart. This command captures a 30-second CPU flamegraph and writes it as an interactive HTML file.

```bash
./profiler.sh -d 30 -f flamegraph.html 12345
```

For JDK Flight Recorder, the equivalent uses jcmd, available since JDK 11 with no external dependencies.

```bash
jcmd 12345 JFR.start duration=30s filename=recording.jfr
```

Open the flamegraph in a browser and read from bottom (entry points like `Thread.run`) to top (leaf methods where CPU time is actually consumed). Width at the top of the stack indicates time spent executing that specific method — not just passing through it as a caller. Focus on these categories of unexpected width: **serialization** frames (Jackson, Gson), **JDBC** driver frames, **lock contention** visible as `AbstractQueuedSynchronizer` frames, and **GC** frames like `G1CollectedHeap` indicating allocation pressure.

The common mistake is chasing deep stacks rather than wide tops. A method appearing in many call paths but individually fast is not your bottleneck — the widest leaf frame is.

sections.title: From Hot Method to Root Cause: APM Correlation and Continuous Profiling
sections.content:
A flamegraph tells you which method is expensive but not which user request pays the cost. Correlating profiler output with **APM traces** from Datadog, Jaeger, or OpenTelemetry closes this gap. Map the hot method from the flamegraph to the service span where it executes, and you know the exact endpoint, the request volume, and the business impact. This turns a performance observation into an actionable ticket with clear ownership.

For continuous production profiling, tools like **Pyroscope** or Datadog's continuous profiler run async-profiler permanently at low sampling rates, storing flamegraphs time-aligned with your distributed traces. This eliminates the scramble to attach a profiler during an incident — the data is already there when you need it. The overhead stays below 1%, making it viable even for latency-sensitive services.

The critical discipline is re-profiling after every fix. Performance work without before-and-after flamegraphs is guesswork with a commit message. The profiler should show the previously wide frame narrowed or gone entirely. If the hot frame did not shrink, the fix did not work — regardless of how confident you were in the code change.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **async-profiler generates flamegraphs with minimal production overhead** — safe for 30-60s production profiling; widest boxes at the flamegraph top are the hottest call paths; download and run without JVM restart
- **JFR captures allocation, GC, and thread events** — `jcmd PID JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr`; built into JDK, near-zero overhead; open in JDK Mission Control for allocation and GC analysis
- **Heap dump + Eclipse MAT Dominator Tree for memory leaks** — `jmap -dump:live` captures live objects; Dominator Tree shows what's retaining heap; growing instance count per request = leak
- **Three thread dumps at 5-second intervals for blocking** — threads consistently in BLOCKED state across all three dumps are genuinely blocked; transient contention appears only in one dump
- **Profile before optimizing** — changing code based on intuition fixes the wrong thing; the actual bottleneck is almost never where you expect; measure first, change second

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Profiling a Java application starts with measuring before changing anything — a flamegraph or thread dump tells you where time is actually spent, which is almost never where you expect.

**CPU profiling with async-profiler**
- async-profiler samples the call stack at regular intervals without the overhead of traditional JVMTI profilers — which means it's safe to run in production for short periods without perceptibly increasing latency
- `./profiler.sh -d 30 -f flamegraph.html PID` captures 30 seconds and generates an interactive flamegraph; the widest boxes at the top of the flamegraph are the methods consuming the most CPU
- Common CPU hotspots in Spring Boot: JSON serialization/deserialization in a tight loop (recreating ObjectMapper), Hibernate N+1 generating thousands of SQL calls, string concatenation in logging without a guard

**Memory profiling with JFR**
- Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is built into the JDK and has near-zero overhead — `jcmd PID JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr` captures allocation, GC, thread events, and more for 60 seconds
- Open the recording in JDK Mission Control; the Allocation tab shows which call sites allocate the most objects; the GC tab shows pause durations and frequencies
- Short-lived objects that escape to old gen are the most common memory footprint problem — they force more frequent full GCs

**Heap dump analysis**
- When you suspect a memory leak: `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof PID` captures a heap snapshot; open in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM
- The "Dominator Tree" in Eclipse MAT shows the objects retaining the most heap; a class whose instance count grows with each request indicates a leak (typically static collections, unclosed resources, or ThreadLocal values)

**Thread dump for deadlock and blocking**
- `jstack PID` or `kill -3 PID` generates a thread dump; look for threads in BLOCKED state (contended lock) or WAITING state (waiting indefinitely); a stack trace showing all threads blocked on the same monitor is a deadlock
- Repeat the thread dump 3 times at 5-second intervals — threads consistently blocked on the same call stack across all three dumps are real blocking, not transient waits

questions.question: How do you size thread pools for optimal throughput?
questions.title: Sizing Thread Pools for Optimal Throughput

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Little's Law and the CPU vs. I/O-bound distinction, and can apply them to real pool sizing decisions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an arbitrary number like 10 or 100 without reasoning, or ignoring the wait-to-compute ratio for I/O-bound work.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Little's Law explicitly and mention dynamic pool sizing with metrics feedback loops or using virtual threads (Project Loom) for I/O-bound workloads.

questions.direct_answer: For CPU-bound work set pool size to N+1 cores; for I/O-bound work use Little's Law: threads = target_concurrency x (1 + wait_time / compute_time), then tune empirically.

sections.title: Why 'More Threads' Usually Makes Things Worse
sections.content:
Pick a number — say, 200 threads. It feels safe, right? Enough capacity for traffic spikes, enough headroom for slow requests. In practice, those 200 threads create 200-way contention for CPU cores, blow the CPU cache working set, and generate thousands of context switches per second. The application gets slower as you add threads beyond the optimal point, not faster.

Thread pool sizing is not about picking a large-enough number. It is about matching the pool to the nature of the work. **CPU-bound work** — data transformation, encryption, image processing — benefits from exactly as many threads as there are cores, because adding more means the OS must constantly swap them on and off cores. **I/O-bound work** — database calls, HTTP requests, file reads — spends most of its time waiting, so more threads can usefully overlap those wait periods.

The mathematical foundation is **Little's Law**: concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by average service time. In thread pool terms, the number of threads you need equals the request rate you want to sustain multiplied by how long each request holds a thread. This formula is the starting point for every sizing decision — not a guess, not a copy-paste from a blog post, and definitely not the default 200 that Spring Boot ships with.

sections.title: The CPU-Bound Formula: cores + 1 and Why It Is a Ceiling
sections.content:
When every thread is doing pure computation — no I/O waits, no blocking calls — adding threads beyond the number of CPU cores creates pure overhead. Each additional thread means the OS scheduler must preempt a running thread, save its register state, restore another thread's state, and invalidate CPU cache lines. On a 4-core machine, this starts happening at thread 5.

The standard formula is **cores + 1**. The extra thread compensates for the occasional page fault or scheduling hiccup that idles a core momentarily.

```java
int cpuPoolSize = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + 1;
ExecutorService cpuPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cpuPoolSize);
```

This pool stays efficient because every thread has a core to run on without contention. Going beyond this — say, 16 threads on 4 cores — means four threads run while twelve wait, and every context switch wastes 5-10 microseconds that compounds under sustained load.

In container environments, be aware that `availableProcessors()` respects CPU limits set by cgroups since JDK 10. A container with a 2-core limit correctly returns 2, not the host's 64 cores. Before JDK 10, this function returned the host core count, causing massive over-provisioning inside containers.

sections.title: The I/O-Bound Formula: Little's Law Applied to Thread Pools
When Formulas Fail: Empirical Tuning and Virtual Threads
sections.content:
Formulas produce a good starting point but not the final answer. Production workloads shift with traffic patterns, downstream latency changes, and seasonal demand. The only way to find the true optimal pool size is to **load test throughput against thread count** and look for the knee point — where adding threads no longer increases throughput but starts increasing tail latency.

Graph requests-per-second on the Y axis and thread count on the X axis. Throughput climbs, flattens, then drops. The optimal point is just before the plateau, where you get maximum throughput without the p99 latency penalty.

For dynamic adjustment, expose pool metrics through **Micrometer** — active count, queue depth, and task latency histograms. Set alerts when queue depth grows steadily, which indicates the pool is undersized for the sustained arrival rate. Spring's `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` supports `setCorePoolSize()` at runtime, allowing pool resizing without redeployment.

**Virtual threads** (Java 21) eliminate manual I/O-bound pool sizing entirely. A virtual thread parks cheaply when blocked on I/O, consuming no OS thread. You create one virtual thread per task with `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` and let the JVM scheduler manage concurrency. The CPU-bound formula still applies to compute-heavy work, but for services dominated by database and HTTP calls, virtual threads make pool sizing a non-problem.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CPU-bound: `cores + 1`; I/O-bound: Little's Law (`throughput x latency`)** — more threads than cores for CPU work adds context-switching overhead; I/O-bound work needs more threads because most of them are blocked at any time
- **Little's Law for HTTP services: `threads = RPS x avg_latency_seconds`** — 200 req/s x 0.1s = 20 threads needed; Spring Boot's default 200 Tomcat threads handles most OLTP services; measure before changing
- **`tomcat.threads.busy / tomcat.threads.config.max > 0.8` = pool saturation** — threads are consistently busy; either increase max-threads (if I/O-bound) or reduce per-request latency (if CPU-bound)
- **`@Async` pools are separate from Tomcat** — `spring.task.execution.pool.max-size` controls the `@Async` thread pool; a full `@Async` pool blocks callers in the calling thread; size it based on the async work's I/O ratio
- **Virtual threads (Java 21) change the model for I/O-bound work** — virtual threads are cheap; configure Tomcat to use virtual threads with `server.tomcat.use-virtual-threads=true`; thread pool sizing becomes less critical because virtual threads park instead of block

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Thread pool sizing comes down to whether the work is CPU-bound or I/O-bound — the right formula is different for each, and most Java backend services are I/O-bound.

**CPU-bound work**
- CPU-bound work uses the CPU continuously — computing a hash, parsing a large document, running a machine learning inference; the thread can't go faster than the CPU allows
- For CPU-bound pools: `pool size = number of CPU cores + 1`; the extra thread covers the brief moments a CPU thread is paused (GC, OS scheduling); more threads than this causes context-switching overhead that reduces throughput

**I/O-bound work — Little's Law**
- I/O-bound work spends most of its time waiting — waiting for a database query, an HTTP call, a file read; the thread is blocked and the CPU is free
- Little's Law: `pool size = throughput x average latency`; if the target is 200 requests/second and each request blocks for 100ms on I/O, you need `200 x 0.1 = 20` threads to keep all 20 blocked threads covered
- In practice for a Tomcat thread pool: start with `max-threads = 200` for a typical Spring Boot service; measure thread pool saturation (active threads approaching max) under load and adjust

**Spring Boot thread pool configuration**
- `server.tomcat.threads.max` (default 200): the maximum number of request-handling threads; increase if threads are consistently saturated during load tests
- `server.tomcat.accept-count` (default 100): the accept queue size; when all threads are busy, new connections queue here; if the queue fills, connections are refused
- `spring.task.execution.pool.max-size` for `@Async` method pools; `spring.task.scheduling.pool.size` for `@Scheduled` tasks — these are separate from Tomcat's request thread pool

**Measuring saturation**
- Micrometer exposes `tomcat.threads.busy` and `tomcat.threads.config.max`; `busy / max > 0.8` consistently means the thread pool is saturated; increase max-threads or reduce per-request latency (faster DB queries, connection pooling)

questions.question: How do you diagnose and fix a slow database query in a Spring Boot app?
questions.title: Diagnosing and Fixing Slow Database Queries in Spring Boot

interviewer_intent.testing: Your ability to systematically diagnose slow queries end-to-end — from detection in logs through query analysis to code-level and schema-level fixes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Going straight to adding an index without checking the execution plan, or fixing the symptom without understanding the cause.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention enabling slow query logs, using EXPLAIN ANALYZE, checking for N+1 with Hibernate statistics, and adding covering indexes vs. partial indexes based on the query pattern.

questions.direct_answer: Enable slow query logging, capture the query, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, identify missing indexes or N+1 patterns, fix at the query or schema level, and verify with re-execution.

sections.title: The Slow Endpoint That Is Actually Hundreds of Fast Queries
sections.content:
A Spring Boot endpoint returns order data in 3 seconds under moderate load. The database server shows low CPU and no slow query log entries. The team suspects the query needs an index, but adding one changes nothing — because the problem is not one slow query. It is **101 fast queries** executing sequentially.

This is the N+1 query problem, and it is the most common database performance issue in Spring Boot applications using Hibernate. The ORM fires one query to fetch the parent entities, then one query per parent to lazy-load each child collection. Each individual query takes 10ms — fast enough to avoid the slow query log — but 101 of them take a full second. Under concurrency, connection pool contention amplifies this to 3 seconds or more.

The dangerous aspect of N+1 is invisibility. Without Hibernate statistics enabled, the application logs show nothing wrong. The database metrics look normal because individual query execution time is fine. The problem only surfaces as unexplained latency that gets worse with data volume — 100 orders means 101 queries, 1000 orders means 1001 queries.

sections.title: The Lazy-Loading Default That Hibernate Sets as a Trap
Following the Evidence: From Invisible Queries to EXPLAIN ANALYZE
sections.content:
The first step is making the N+1 visible. Enable Hibernate statistics and SQL logging in `application.properties`.

```properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.stat=DEBUG
```

With statistics enabled, Hibernate logs a summary after each session: the number of SQL statements prepared, the number of queries executed, and the entity fetch count. An entry like `101 JDBC statements executed` for a single endpoint call is the smoking gun.

Run **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** on the repeated child query directly in your database to understand its individual cost. If the planner shows a sequential scan instead of an index scan on the foreign key column, that is the second problem to fix — even after solving N+1, the remaining JOIN query will be slow without the index.

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM line_items WHERE order_id = 42;
-- Look for: Seq Scan (bad) vs Index Scan (good)
-- Check rows estimated vs rows actual for plan accuracy
```

For deeper investigation, use **p6spy** or Spring Boot Actuator JDBC metrics to count prepared statements per request in staging. If the statement count scales linearly with the number of parent entities, N+1 is confirmed and the fix path is clear.

sections.title: One Query Instead of One Hundred: JOIN FETCH and Proper Indexing
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Count SQL statements per request first** — more than 10 for a simple endpoint indicates N+1; Hibernate's SQL logging makes the pattern immediately visible without any tracing setup
- **`JOIN FETCH` for single collection N+1; `@BatchSize` for multiple collections** — `JOIN FETCH` loads one collection eagerly in the initial query; `@BatchSize(size=25)` loads multiple collections in IN-list batches without Cartesian product
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` reveals missing indexes** — `Seq Scan` on a large table = no index; `Index Only Scan` = covering index in use; `actual rows` vs `estimated rows` discrepancy = stale statistics
- **`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` adds indexes without table locks** — standard `CREATE INDEX` locks the table; `CONCURRENTLY` builds the index in the background while reads and writes continue
- **`hibernate.generate_statistics=true` reports total query count and time** — logs at session close; shows queries per request; total time breakdown between in-memory and database operations

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When a Spring Boot endpoint is slow and the database is involved, the first suspects are always N+1 queries and missing indexes. These two problems cause the majority of database-related latency in Spring Boot applications.

**Step 1 — Enable SQL logging**
- `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` and `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG` log every SQL statement; `logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE` logs parameter values
- Count the number of SQL statements for a single HTTP request — more than 5-10 for a simple read suggests N+1; one query per entity in a collection fetch is the giveaway pattern

**Detecting N+1**
- The symptom: fetching 50 orders generates 51 SQL statements — 1 for the orders list, 50 for their items; Hibernate's lazy loading triggers a SELECT per entity
- Fix: `JOIN FETCH` in JPQL: `SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items WHERE o.status = 'ACTIVE'`; or `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items"})` on the repository method; or `@BatchSize(size = 25)` for collections that can't be JOIN FETCHed without a Cartesian product

**Detecting missing indexes**
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (PostgreSQL) or `EXPLAIN` (MySQL) on the slow query; look for `Seq Scan` (PostgreSQL) or `type: ALL` (MySQL) on large tables — these mean no index was used
- Add an index on the WHERE clause column: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON orders(customer_id)` in PostgreSQL; verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the plan changes to `Index Scan` or `Index Only Scan`

**Slow query log**
- `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true` logs query count and time per session; configure the database's slow query log to capture queries taking over 1 second
- Capture the slow query and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a database client with realistic data; the execution plan on a test database with 100 rows doesn't reveal the plan the production database with 50M rows uses

questions.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput and how do you optimize each?
questions.title: Latency vs Throughput: Definitions and Optimization Strategies

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that latency and throughput are often in tension and that optimizing one can harm the other without careful design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as the same thing or assuming that faster individual requests always means better throughput.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the latency-throughput trade-off using queuing theory, mention percentile latency (p99) vs average, and give concrete Java-level examples for each axis.

questions.direct_answer: Latency is time per request; throughput is requests per second. Optimize latency by reducing per-request work (caching, async I/O); optimize throughput by maximizing concurrency and batching.

sections.title: The Trade-Off Engineers Keep Getting Wrong
sections.content:
Latency and throughput feel like two sides of the same coin — make requests faster and you handle more of them, right? Not always. **Batching** database writes increases throughput by amortizing per-call overhead, but each individual write waits longer because it sits in a batch queue. Adding an in-memory **cache** reduces latency for cache hits to microseconds, but a cold cache under a traffic spike can collapse throughput as thousands of requests stampede to the origin. Optimizing one metric without watching the other leads to outages.

The relationship is governed by **Little's Law**: `L = λ × W`, where L is concurrency (in-flight requests), λ is throughput (requests per second), and W is average latency (seconds per request). Rearranged: throughput equals concurrency divided by latency. This means you can increase throughput by adding concurrency — more threads, more connections — even if per-request latency stays the same. But this only works until contention for shared resources (CPU cores, database locks, connection pool slots) starts increasing both latency and failure rate simultaneously.

The critical distinction for production systems is that latency must be measured in **percentiles** (p50, p95, p99), not averages. A service with 10ms average latency and 500ms p99 is not a 10ms service — it is a service where 1 in 100 users waits half a second. GC pauses, lock contention, and connection pool exhaustion all hide in the average but dominate the tail. Averaging latency across requests is like averaging temperature across seasons — the number is correct and completely useless for deciding what to wear today.

sections.title: Two Metrics, Two Different Optimization Strategies
sections.content:
The core distinction plays out across every dimension of system design. Understanding which metric matters for your use case determines whether you invest engineering effort in caching and reducing hops, or in batching and parallelism. A service optimized for throughput that ignores tail latency will lose users to perceived slowness. A service optimized for latency at the expense of throughput will need twice the infrastructure to handle the same load.

| Dimension | Latency | Throughput |
|---|---|---|
| **What it measures** | Time for one operation to complete | Operations completed per second |
| **Unit** | ms, μs | req/s, TPS |
| **Who feels it** | Individual user waiting for a response | Capacity planners sizing infrastructure |
| **Key metric** | p99 latency (not average) | Max sustained RPS under SLA |
| **Primary levers** | Caching, async I/O, reduce serial hops | Batching, parallelism, pool sizing |
| **Danger of over-optimizing** | No batching reduces throughput | Queuing increases tail latency |
| **Common bottleneck** | Sequential blocking calls on critical path | Undersized thread or connection pools |
| **Measurement tool** | HDR histogram, percentile time-series | Load test with sustained RPS ramp |

The relationship between the two columns is not symmetry — it is tension. The levers that improve one column often degrade the other, which is why sizing decisions require explicit trade-off conversations rather than default configurations.

sections.title: When to Prioritize Each — and When You Need Both
sections.content:
**Optimize for latency first** when you serve interactive user-facing requests. A user waiting for a page load experiences p99 latency, not throughput numbers on a dashboard. The levers are reducing serial blocking calls on the critical path, caching frequently accessed data to skip expensive computation, and parallelizing independent I/O calls with `CompletableFuture.allOf()`. Measure with **HDR Histogram** and alert on p99 crossing your SLA threshold — average latency alerts fire too late because the tail has already degraded for real users.

**Optimize for throughput first** when you process batch jobs, event streams, or ETL pipelines where per-item latency is less important than total completion time. The levers are batching database writes to amortize per-call overhead, right-sizing thread and connection pools to maximize concurrent work, and removing serialization bottlenecks. Measure sustained requests per second under realistic load, and size infrastructure for your peak traffic multiplier.

**Both matter simultaneously** in API gateways, databases, and any service with both a latency SLA and a throughput capacity target. The design pattern is **load shedding**: accept requests only up to the throughput level that maintains acceptable latency. Return HTTP 503 for excess traffic rather than queuing it and degrading latency for everyone. Backpressure in reactive frameworks like Project Reactor achieves this automatically with operators like `onBackpressureDrop()`.

The queuing theory insight that ties everything together is that **latency degrades exponentially as utilization approaches 100%**. At 50% utilization, queuing delay is manageable. At 90%, every request waits significantly longer. This is why production services target 60-70% utilization — enough headroom to absorb traffic spikes without latency collapsing into cascading timeouts.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Latency = time per request; throughput = requests per second** — optimizing one may not optimize the other; measure both separately; a cache improves latency AND throughput; a larger thread pool improves throughput only
- **Identify the bottleneck before optimizing** — flamegraph for CPU bottleneck; EXPLAIN ANALYZE for database bottleneck; thread dump for lock contention; thread pool metrics for saturation; fix the actual bottleneck
- **Caching improves both latency and throughput** — latency drops from milliseconds (DB query) to microseconds (Redis read); throughput increases because fewer requests reach the database; highest-leverage single change for read-heavy services
- **Reactive I/O (WebFlux) improves throughput, not necessarily latency** — eliminates the thread-per-request model; handles more concurrent requests with fewer threads; individual request latency may be similar or higher than blocking I/O
- **Batching trades latency for throughput** — writing 100 rows in one transaction instead of 100 separate transactions; database throughput increases; each row waits longer; appropriate for async write paths, not user-facing requests

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Latency and throughput measure different things and are optimized differently — which means a change that reduces latency may increase throughput, reduce it, or have no effect, depending on where the bottleneck is.

**The definitions**
- Latency is how long one request takes — the user's wait from sending the request to receiving the response; measured in milliseconds per request; P99 latency is the experience of the worst-affected 1% of users
- Throughput is how many requests the system handles per unit of time — requests per second; the ceiling is determined by the bottleneck resource (CPU, I/O, threads, connection pool)

**Latency optimization — reduce per-request work**
- Eliminate unnecessary operations on the critical path: a database query that joins five tables when only two columns are needed; a synchronous HTTP call to a dependency that could be async; JSON deserialization of a large payload when only one field is used
- Caching: serve responses from Redis in microseconds instead of database queries in milliseconds; the first request is slow, every subsequent one is fast
- Reduce serialization overhead: Jackson ObjectMapper is expensive to construct; singleton ObjectMapper with specific features disabled; faster serializers like Jackson Afterburner or custom serializers for hot paths

**Throughput optimization — remove the bottleneck**
- Throughput is limited by the bottleneck resource; increasing throughput means identifying and removing that bottleneck
- If the bottleneck is the thread pool (threads saturated): add more threads (if I/O-bound) or reduce per-request CPU work; or switch to reactive/non-blocking I/O (WebFlux) which eliminates thread-per-request
- If the bottleneck is the database: add read replicas, add indexes, implement caching; the database often becomes the bottleneck before the application does

**The trade-offs**
- Batching increases throughput at the cost of latency — batching 100 writes in one database transaction reduces I/O but each write waits until the batch is full
- Parallelism reduces latency (fan-out multiple I/O calls) at the cost of more threads — `CompletableFuture.allOf()` runs multiple downstream calls in parallel; each call uses a thread

questions.question: How do you reduce Java application memory footprint?
questions.title: Reducing Java Application Memory Footprint

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish heap from off-heap memory and apply multiple complementary techniques to reduce total process memory.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only adjusting -Xmx without understanding that JVM native memory, metaspace, and off-heap buffers also contribute to total RSS.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention GraalVM native image for startup and memory reduction, class data sharing (AppCDS), and profiling allocation with async-profiler in allocation mode.

questions.direct_answer: Profile allocations first, then reduce heap with object pooling and smaller data structures, tune GC settings, limit metaspace, and consider GraalVM native image for dramatic RSS reduction.

sections.title: Why -Xmx Is Only Half the Story
sections.content:
Your pod gets OOM-killed even though `-Xmx=512m` should fit comfortably inside a 1GB container limit. The JVM's total memory — reported by the OS as **RSS** (Resident Set Size) — includes much more than the heap: **metaspace** for class metadata (typically 50-200MB), **code cache** for JIT-compiled native code (up to 240MB by default), **thread stacks** where each thread consumes 512KB-1MB, **direct ByteBuffers** used by NIO and Netty, and internal JVM structures like GC bookkeeping.

A Spring Boot microservice with `-Xmx=256m` running 200 Tomcat threads can easily consume 600MB+ of RSS. The heap is 256MB, but 200 thread stacks at 512KB each add another 100MB, metaspace adds 80MB, and code cache adds 50MB more. Kubernetes sees the RSS, compares it to the container memory limit, and kills the pod if it exceeds the limit — regardless of what `-Xmx` says.

Reducing memory footprint requires profiling where the bytes actually are — heap, off-heap, or native — and applying different techniques to each region. Guessing which component to shrink wastes effort and risks breaking things you did not intend to touch.

sections.title: Finding the Top Allocation Sites Before Changing Anything
sections.content:
Async-profiler in allocation mode reveals which call sites create the most objects, showing you exactly where heap pressure originates before you change a single line of code.

```bash
./profiler.sh -d 30 -e alloc -f alloc-flamegraph.html 12345
```

The allocation flamegraph works like a CPU flamegraph but measures object allocation bytes instead of CPU time. The widest frames at the top represent the call sites that allocate the most — typically three to five sites account for 80% of allocation pressure.

Common findings include: **byte array allocations** from reading HTTP request bodies or database result sets, **String concatenation** in logging or serialization paths creating intermediate objects, and **autoboxing** from using `Map<Integer, Long>` where primitives would suffice.

For a complete picture of non-heap memory, use **Native Memory Tracking** by starting the JVM with `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` and querying with `jcmd <PID> VM.native_memory summary`. This shows metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, and internal memory separately — the exact breakdown you need to know which lever to pull.

sections.title: Heap Hygiene: Primitives, Buffer Reuse, and String Deduplication
sections.content:
The most effective heap reductions target the top allocation sites identified by the profiler. Replace **boxed types** with primitives where possible — an `Integer` object occupies 16 bytes on 64-bit JVMs versus 4 bytes for an `int`. Libraries like **Eclipse Collections** and **Koloboke** provide primitive-typed maps and sets that eliminate autoboxing entirely for large collections.

For services that process request bodies or database result sets, **reuse byte arrays** through a pool instead of allocating per request. Netty's `PooledByteBufAllocator` does this automatically for network I/O, and you can apply the same pattern in application code with a simple `ThreadLocal<byte[]>` for fixed-size buffers.

Enable **string deduplication** with `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` on the G1 collector. When heap dumps show many duplicate string values — common in services that process repeated fields like country codes, status values, or product categories — G1 deduplicates their backing `char[]` arrays during GC, often recovering 10-20% of heap.

Set `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx` to avoid heap resizing overhead. When the heap grows, the JVM allocates new memory regions and copies live objects, creating a latency spike that resembles a long GC pause.

sections.title: Structural Changes: Metaspace Caps, Stack Tuning, and GraalVM
sections.content:
Beyond the heap, cap **metaspace** with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m` to prevent classloader leaks from growing unboundedly. Spring Boot applications with dynamic proxies and frameworks like Groovy or Velocity can leak metaspace slowly over days. Without a cap, the leak grows until the OS kills the process — often at 3 AM, weeks after the leaking code was deployed.

Reduce thread **stack size** with `-Xss256k` when running hundreds of threads. The default (512KB on Linux, 1MB on macOS) is generous for most application threads. This saves 50-75MB on a service running 200 threads — memory that was reserved but rarely used.

For services where memory density is critical — serverless functions, sidecar containers, high-density Kubernetes clusters — evaluate **GraalVM native image**. Ahead-of-time compilation eliminates the JIT compiler, code cache, and most metaspace overhead. RSS drops from 300-600MB to 30-60MB. Startup drops from seconds to milliseconds. The trade-off is a longer build step and restrictions on reflection and dynamic class loading — Spring Boot 3+ supports native image through its AOT processing engine.

**AppCDS** (Application Class Data Sharing) is a lighter alternative that caches parsed class metadata in a shared archive file, reducing per-process metaspace in multi-JVM deployments by 10-20MB per instance without the AOT constraints.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JVM RSS includes heap + metaspace + JIT code + direct memory + stacks** — `-Xmx` controls only heap; a JVM with `-Xmx512m` can consume 1GB+ of RSS; profile total memory consumption, not just heap
- **JFR Allocation tab finds the high-allocation call sites** — allocation in a hot path causes frequent GC pauses; fix by object pooling, reusing collections with initial capacity, or avoiding unnecessary intermediate objects
- **`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` in containers instead of fixed `-Xmx`** — adapts to the container's memory limit; prevents OOM kills when the limit is changed without updating the JVM flag; the idiomatic approach for Spring Boot in Kubernetes
- **Metaspace leak from dynamic class loading** — set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m` to cap it; OOM on metaspace reveals the leak; common in apps that use CGLIB proxies excessively or generate dynamic classes
- **Object pooling for expensive-to-create, safe-to-reuse objects** — database connections (HikariCP), byte buffers (Netty), and large domain objects with expensive initialization; pooling reduces GC pressure on old gen

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java's memory footprint is larger than most developers expect because the JVM RSS (Resident Set Size) includes heap, metaspace, JIT-compiled code, direct memory, and thread stacks — setting `-Xmx` controls only one of these.

**Profile allocations before optimizing**
- Use JFR's Allocation tab or async-profiler's allocation mode to find the code paths allocating the most objects — which tells you where object creation is excessive before you make any changes
- Common high-allocation culprits: `String.format()` in hot paths (use `+` concatenation or avoid entirely), `new ArrayList()` inside loops without initial capacity, creating `ObjectMapper` per request

**Reducing heap usage**
- Object pooling: reuse expensive objects instead of creating and GCing them — Apache Commons Pool for database connections, Netty's ByteBuf pooling for byte buffers, object pools for frequently created domain objects with expensive initialization
- Smaller data structures: `int[]` instead of `List<Integer>` eliminates boxing overhead; `HashMap` with initial capacity set avoids resize operations; prefer primitive types in hot-path code
- Shorter object lifetimes: objects that survive two young GC collections get promoted to old gen; reduce the lifetime of large objects (close resources eagerly, don't cache unnecessarily)

**Reducing off-heap memory**
- Metaspace holds class metadata — an application that dynamically loads classes (e.g., via reflection, Groovy scripts, or dynamic proxies) can leak metaspace; set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m` to cap it and surface leaks as `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`
- Direct memory is used by NIO, Netty, and heap-bypassing serializers — pool and reuse ByteBuffers; allocating and releasing large ByteBuffers repeatedly causes slow off-heap fragmentation

**JVM flags for smaller footprint**
- `-XX:+UseSerialGC` or `-XX:+UseG1GC` depending on latency requirements; for containers: `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` instead of a fixed `-Xmx` so the JVM adapts to the container's memory limit automatically
- `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` disables the JIT compiler's highest optimization tier — reduces memory used by JIT code caches at the cost of some throughput; useful for short-lived Lambda functions or batch jobs

questions.question: What causes CPU spikes in Java applications and how do you debug them?
questions.title: Diagnosing CPU Spikes in Java Applications

interviewer_intent.testing: Your ability to distinguish between expected CPU spikes (GC, JIT compilation) and pathological ones (hot loops, lock contention), and to use the right tools to diagnose each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Restarting the application instead of capturing a thread dump or flamegraph while the spike is happening, losing all diagnostic information.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention capturing thread dumps during the spike, correlating with GC logs, and using async-profiler wall-clock mode to catch I/O-induced CPU spikes from busy-wait patterns.

questions.direct_answer: Capture a flamegraph and thread dump during the spike; common causes are GC pressure, hot loops, lock contention, or JIT compilation bursts — each has a distinct signature.

sections.title: The Spike That Disappears When You Restart — Taking the Evidence With It
sections.content:
A Java microservice periodically spikes to 100% CPU for 5-10 seconds, then recovers. Users experience timeouts during the spike, the on-call engineer restarts the pod, and the problem disappears — along with all diagnostic evidence. The team opens a ticket, marks it as intermittent, and moves on. Three days later, it happens again.

The worst response to a CPU spike is restarting the process. Thread stacks, heap state, JIT compilation state, and GC logs all live in process memory. Once the process dies, the only evidence left is external metrics that show the spike happened but not why.

The correct response is to capture data while the spike is live: a **thread dump** shows what each thread is doing at that moment, a **CPU flamegraph** shows which methods consume the most time, and **GC logs** differentiate between application CPU usage and garbage collection overhead. Together, these three artifacts usually identify the root cause in minutes rather than the weeks of guesswork that follow a blind restart.

sections.title: The Busy-Wait and the Regex Bomb: Two Classic CPU Thieves
Capturing the Smoking Gun While the Spike Is Live
sections.content:
The moment you see a CPU spike on monitoring, start capturing data — do not restart. Run these commands in sequence.

```bash
# Find which threads are consuming CPU (note thread IDs in hex)
top -H -p <PID>

# Capture thread dump — shows what each thread is doing right now
jstack <PID> > threaddump.txt

# Capture CPU flamegraph for 10 seconds
./profiler.sh -d 10 -e cpu -f spike.html <PID>

# Check if GC is the culprit — watch Full GC frequency
jstat -gcutil <PID> 1000
```

Match the hot thread IDs from `top -H` (converted to hexadecimal) against the thread names in the jstack dump. If the hot thread is stuck in a tight loop, you will see it in RUNNABLE state executing the same method repeatedly.

The flamegraph provides a broader view — it shows all threads' CPU consumption, not just the hottest one. Each root cause has a distinct signature: **busy-wait** shows a single narrow deep stack with one method consuming all the width. **GC thrashing** shows wide `G1CollectedHeap` or `ParallelGC` frames. **ReDoS** shows deep `java.util.regex.Pattern$GroupHead` frames. **JIT compilation** bursts show `C2 CompilerThread` frames prominently during the first minutes after deployment.

For spikes that appear only under specific traffic patterns, use async-profiler in **wall-clock mode** (`-e wall`). Standard CPU sampling misses threads that are blocked on I/O or parked on locks — wall-clock mode samples all threads regardless of state, revealing I/O-induced CPU spikes that CPU-only profiling misses.

sections.title: Exponential Backoff and Safe Regex: Fixing the Two Most Common Causes
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Capture flamegraph before restarting** — restarting clears the running stack; async-profiler captures CPU samples in 30 seconds without stopping the JVM; widest boxes at the top = hottest methods
- **`jstat -gcutil PID 1000` for GC-caused CPU spikes** — shows Young GC frequency and Old Gen usage in real time; Old Gen approaching 100% precedes a full GC pause; `GCT` column shows cumulative GC time
- **Hot locks show as thread pileups on the same frame** — many threads in the flamegraph on the same `lock()` or `synchronized` call; confirm with `jstack PID` showing threads in BLOCKED state on the same monitor
- **Regex `Pattern.compile()` in hot paths is CPU-intensive** — pre-compile patterns as `static final Pattern PATTERN = Pattern.compile(...)` at class initialization; constructor-scope or request-scope compilation adds measurable CPU overhead
- **JIT compilation spike at startup is expected** — `CompilerThread` frames in the flamegraph during the first minutes of traffic; subsides after the JVM warms up; if it persists, the application is loading new classes continuously (dynamic proxy creation)

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When CPU spikes in a Java application, the most important thing is to capture data before restarting — a restart clears the evidence and you're left guessing.

**Capture a flamegraph during the spike**
- `./profiler.sh -d 30 -f spike.html PID` captures a 30-second CPU flamegraph while the spike is happening — the widest boxes at the top of the flamegraph are the methods consuming the most CPU during the spike
- async-profiler doesn't require the application to be stopped or restarted; it's safe to run in production briefly

**Common causes visible in flamegraphs**
- GC pressure: the flamegraph shows the GC threads consuming a large fraction of CPU — confirm with `jstat -gcutil PID 1000` which shows GC pauses and heap usage in real time; if Old Gen usage is climbing toward 100%, a full GC is imminent
- Hot locks: many threads piling up on a `synchronized` block or `ReentrantLock`; the flamegraph shows all threads in the same lock-acquire call path; a `jstack PID` at the same time shows threads in BLOCKED state
- Compilation: the JVM's JIT compiler compiles hot methods; a cold-start CPU spike often shows `Interpreter` and `CompilerThread` frames; this is expected and subsides as the JVM warms up
- Regex compilation: `Pattern.compile()` in a hot path is CPU-intensive; compile patterns at class initialization and store as static final fields

**GC-related CPU spikes**
- Young GC pauses are frequent but short (< 50ms); high young GC frequency means the application is allocating objects faster than the young gen can be collected; increase Eden size or reduce allocations
- Old Gen full GC is the severe case — `jstat -gcutil PID` shows `O` column approaching 100% before the spike; the full GC pause causes a CPU spike as all application threads stop; look for memory leaks or over-caching

sections.title: The 20-100ms Tax on Every Unpooled Database Call
sections.content:
Every time a Spring Boot application opens a new database connection, it pays for a TCP handshake, TLS negotiation (if enabled), and database authentication. On a local network this costs 20-30ms. Across availability zones, 50-100ms. For a service handling 500 requests per second, establishing a fresh connection per request would add 10-50 seconds of cumulative connection overhead every second — more time than you have.

Connection pooling eliminates this tax by maintaining a set of pre-established connections that are checked out, used, and returned — like library books. The checkout cost drops from tens of milliseconds to **microseconds**. HikariCP, the default connection pool in Spring Boot, is the fastest pool available for Java and the only one most services need.

The counter-intuitive truth about connection pools is that **bigger is not better**. A pool of 100 connections does not make your service 10x faster than a pool of 10. On the database side, each connection consumes memory for session state and can hold locks that block other connections. PostgreSQL's default `max_connections` is 100 — if five service instances each open 30 connections, you are already at the limit. Every connection beyond the optimum adds contention without adding throughput.

sections.title: HikariCP's Counter-Intuitive Sizing Formula
sections.content:
The HikariCP documentation recommends a formula that surprises most engineers: **`pool_size = (cores × 2) + effective_spindle_count`**. For a 4-core application server talking to an SSD-backed database, this gives (4 × 2) + 1 = 9 connections. Not 50. Not 100. Nine.

The reasoning is that database servers achieve maximum throughput with a modest number of concurrent connections executing queries in parallel. Beyond the optimal point, connections compete for disk I/O, CPU, and lock resources, and the database spends more time on context switching than on query execution. PostgreSQL's own benchmarks show throughput peaks at surprisingly low connection counts and degrades as connections increase.

The critical configuration in Spring Boot maps directly to this formula.

```properties
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=3000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=60000
```

Setting `connection-timeout` to 3 seconds makes the application fail fast when the pool is exhausted, rather than blocking every request thread for the default 30 seconds. This turns pool exhaustion from a slow degradation into an immediate, diagnosable error.

sections.title: Three Settings That Prevent Silent Pool Degradation
sections.content:
Beyond pool size, three HikariCP settings separate production-ready configurations from defaults that silently degrade under load.

**`connection-timeout`** controls how long a thread waits for a connection when the pool is empty. The default is 30 seconds — far too long for most services. When the pool is exhausted, every incoming request blocks for 30 seconds before failing. Set this to 3-5 seconds so the application fails fast with a clear error instead of accumulating blocked threads that eventually cascade into a full outage.

**`max-lifetime`** controls how long a connection lives before being recycled. Set this shorter than the database server's own connection timeout to avoid stale connection errors. When the database kills idle connections that the pool still considers alive, the application gets `Communications link failure` storms on the next burst of traffic. For PostgreSQL with default settings, 30 minutes (1800000ms) is a safe value.

**`leak-detection-threshold`** catches application code that checks out a connection and never returns it. Set this to a value slightly above your longest expected query time — typically 60 seconds for OLTP workloads. When triggered, HikariCP logs the full stack trace where the connection was acquired. This is the fastest way to find missing `close()` calls or forgotten transaction boundaries without attaching a debugger.

sections.title: Monitoring Pool Health and Coordinating Across Instances
sections.content:
HikariCP exposes metrics through Micrometer that Spring Boot Actuator surfaces automatically. The metric that matters most for operational health is **`hikaricp.connections.pending`** — the number of threads waiting for a connection. Set an alert when this exceeds zero for more than 30 seconds. This is the earliest signal that the pool is becoming a bottleneck, appearing minutes before users report slowness.

Watch **`hikaricp.connections.active`** alongside your application server's active thread count. If active connections approach `maximumPoolSize` consistently, the pool is saturated. Either queries are taking longer than expected — check database-side metrics like `pg_stat_activity` — or the pool needs to grow.

For services scaled horizontally, pool sizing becomes a coordination problem. Ten pods with `maximumPoolSize=10` means your database must support 100 concurrent connections. PostgreSQL's default `max_connections=100` becomes the exact bottleneck, and adding application instances silently fails to increase throughput because every new pod competes for the same 100 database connections.

The solution is **PgBouncer** as a connection multiplexer between application pools and the database. PgBouncer shares a smaller number of real database connections across a larger number of application pool connections, decoupling horizontal scaling from database connection capacity. Each application instance keeps its HikariCP pool sized at 10, but PgBouncer ensures the database never sees more connections than it can handle.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HikariCP is Spring Boot's default pool** — auto-configured; `spring.datasource.hikari.*` properties; `maximumPoolSize` is the most important setting; default 10 connections is often the right starting point
- **Pool size: `(cores x 2) + spindles` guideline** — for a 4-core database server, roughly 9-10 connections; 100 connections queue at the database CPU without improving throughput; smaller is often better
- **`connectionTimeout: 3000ms` for production** — default 30 seconds; a thread waiting 30s for a connection means users wait 30s; 3-5s fails fast and frees threads before HTTP client timeouts fire
- **`hikaricp.connections.pending > 0` = pool saturation** — threads queuing for connections; either increase pool size or reduce query duration; pending connections add their wait time directly to request latency
- **PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes application connections** — 50 application HikariCP connections to PgBouncer; 5-10 PgBouncer connections to PostgreSQL; reduces PostgreSQL backend process overhead at high application scale

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Connection pooling reuses database connections across requests — creating a new connection involves a TCP handshake, TLS negotiation (if enabled), and database authentication, which takes 10-50ms; for a service handling thousands of requests per minute, that overhead becomes significant.

**What HikariCP does**
- HikariCP creates a fixed number of database connections at startup and keeps them authenticated and ready — when a request needs the database, it borrows a connection from the pool, uses it, and returns it
- Which means the connection overhead occurs once at startup, not on every database call; at 1,000 req/min, that's 1,000 × 10ms = 10 seconds of connection overhead saved per minute without pooling

**Key configuration parameters**
- `maximumPoolSize`: the ceiling on connections; HikariCP's guidance: `(CPU cores x 2) + effective spindle count`; for a 4-core database server, roughly 9-10 connections; a pool of 100 queues at the database CPU without improving throughput
- `minimumIdle`: connections kept alive when idle; set equal to `maximumPoolSize` for fixed-size pools; lower values save connections during idle periods but cause pool scaling on traffic spikes
- `connectionTimeout`: how long a thread waits for a connection from the pool before throwing an exception; default 30 seconds is too long for production HTTP requests; set 3-5 seconds to fail fast

**Monitoring pool health**
- Micrometer exposes HikariCP metrics automatically: `hikaricp.connections.active` (in use), `hikaricp.connections.idle` (available), `hikaricp.connections.pending` (threads waiting for a connection)
- `pending > 0` consistently means threads are waiting — either increase `maximumPoolSize` (if I/O-bound) or reduce query duration; pending connections add latency to every request that waits

**PgBouncer for PostgreSQL at scale**
- At very high connection counts (hundreds of application instances), PostgreSQL's process-per-connection model becomes expensive — PgBouncer sits between the application and PostgreSQL, multiplexing many application connections to a few PostgreSQL connections
- Transaction-mode pooling in PgBouncer holds the PostgreSQL connection only for the duration of a transaction, allowing one PostgreSQL connection to serve many application connections serially

questions.title: Cache Stampede: What It Is and How to Prevent It

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the thundering herd problem at the cache layer and know the probabilistic early expiry and mutex locking techniques to prevent it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that cache TTL alone is sufficient protection, or using a distributed lock without a timeout (risk of deadlock).

questions.direct_answer: Cache stampede happens when many requests simultaneously miss an expired cache entry. Prevent it with mutex locking, probabilistic early expiry, or background refresh before expiration.

sections.title: 500 Threads Hit the Database at the Same Millisecond
sections.content:
A high-traffic e-commerce site caches its product catalog in Redis with a 60-second TTL. During normal traffic, the cache serves thousands of requests per second at microsecond latency. But every 60 seconds — the moment the TTL expires — hundreds of concurrent requests simultaneously discover a cache miss and independently decide to query the database to rebuild the cache.

The database receives 500 identical queries in the same second. CPU spikes to 100%, connection pools exhaust, and the spike cascades into timeouts for unrelated endpoints sharing the same database. The cache eventually rebuilds — 499 of the 500 responses are thrown away because only one can win the write — but the damage is done. Under extreme traffic, this 60-second cycle can cascade into a full outage.

This is a **cache stampede**, also called a thundering herd. The root cause is not the database query being slow or the cache TTL being wrong. The root cause is that every copy of the cached value expires at exactly the same moment, causing synchronized concurrent recomputation that overwhelms the origin.

sections.title: The Naive Cache-Aside That Works Until Traffic Arrives
Why Shared TTL Creates a Synchronized Thundering Herd
sections.content:
The stampede happens because all copies of the cached value share the same expiry timestamp. When that timestamp passes, every request is a miss, and the cache-aside pattern has no coordination mechanism to prevent concurrent recomputation.

Three characteristics make a cache entry vulnerable to stampede: **popularity** (high request rate means more threads hit the miss window), **compute cost** (an expensive database query means each thread ties up a connection and CPU for a long time), and **sharp TTL** (a fixed expiry time means the transition from cached to uncached is instantaneous rather than gradual).

Three prevention strategies exist, each with different trade-offs:

**Distributed mutex** — only one thread fetches from the database; others wait or serve stale data. Simple to implement but adds latency for waiting threads and requires a lock with a TTL to prevent permanent deadlock if the lock holder crashes.

**Background refresh** — a scheduled job refreshes the cache before it expires, so application threads never trigger a database call. Simplest operationally but requires knowing the refresh schedule and wastes compute if the data changes rarely.

**Probabilistic early expiry (XFetch)** — each request randomly decides whether to refresh the cache before TTL, with probability increasing as expiry approaches. Spreads recomputation over time instead of concentrating it at the expiry moment. No locks, no scheduler, but requires more careful tuning.

sections.title: Three Defenses: Mutex Lock, Background Refresh, and Probabilistic Expiry
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Stampede: popular cache entry expires; all concurrent requests hit the database simultaneously** — database receives full request rate for that entry; CPU saturates; persists until cache is repopulated
- **Mutex lock gates database access to one caller** — first caller sets a Redis lock (`SET nx EX`); fills the cache; others wait then read populated value; prevents N concurrent database queries for the same key
- **Probabilistic early expiry prevents synchronized expiry** — refresh probability increases as TTL decreases; cache is refreshed before expiry; no synchronized miss; implementation: if `random() < beta x delta x log(ttl_remaining)`, refresh now
- **Background refresh is the cleanest solution for hot keys** — scheduled job refreshes before expiry; user requests never see a miss; database queried once per TTL period regardless of traffic
- **TTL jitter prevents coordinated stampedes** — `TTL = base + random(0, base * 0.2)` distributes expiry across a window; prevents all keys set at startup from expiring simultaneously

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A cache stampede happens when a popular cache entry expires and many concurrent requests all miss simultaneously, all query the database, and all try to write the same key back — which can take a database from healthy to overloaded in seconds.

**Why it happens**
- At steady state, the cache serves thousands of requests per second for a popular entry; when that entry's TTL expires, all those concurrent requests reach the database simultaneously — the database receives the full request rate for that entry directly
- If the database query is expensive (joining multiple tables, scanning millions of rows), all concurrent threads run it simultaneously; the database CPU saturates, latency spikes, and the storm persists until the cache is repopulated

**Prevention 1 — Mutex lock**
- When the cache misses, acquire a distributed lock before querying the database: `redisTemplate.execute(new RedisCallback<> { ... SET nx EX 10 ... })`; only the thread that acquires the lock queries the database; all other threads wait briefly and then read from the now-populated cache
- The downside: threads that miss the lock must wait; set the lock TTL longer than the database query duration; handle the case where the lock holder fails before populating the cache

**Prevention 2 — Probabilistic early expiry**
- Rather than expiring all at once, each request has a small probability of proactively refreshing the cache before expiry — as the TTL decreases, the probability of early refresh increases
- By the time the cache actually expires, a lucky early request has already refreshed it; expiry never causes a synchronized miss because the value is always refreshed before TTL reaches zero

**Prevention 3 — Background refresh**
- A scheduled background job refreshes cache entries before they expire — user-facing requests always hit a warm cache because expiry happens in the background, not in the request path
- This is the cleanest solution for high-traffic hot keys: the cache is perpetually warm, and the database is queried once per TTL period regardless of traffic volume

**Prevention 4 — TTL jitter**
- If many keys expire at the same time (set at startup with the same TTL), they all stampede together; add a random jitter: `TTL = baseTTL + random(0, baseTTL * 0.2)` distributes expiry across a window

questions.question: How do you benchmark Java code with JMH?
questions.title: Benchmarking Java Code with JMH

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know that naive microbenchmarks in Java are unreliable due to JIT compilation and dead code elimination, and that JMH exists specifically to handle these pitfalls.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a benchmark with System.currentTimeMillis() in a loop without warmup, which measures JIT compilation time and dead code elimination artifacts rather than steady-state performance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain JVM warmup phases, dead code elimination (why Blackhole matters), and how to interpret JMH output including error margins and mode differences (Throughput vs AverageTime).

questions.direct_answer: JMH handles JVM warmup and dead code elimination that make naive benchmarks unreliable; annotate with @Benchmark, run with sufficient warmup iterations, and use Blackhole to prevent DCE.

sections.title: Why System.nanoTime() Loops Measure the Wrong Thing
sections.content:
Writing `long start = System.nanoTime()` before a loop and computing the elapsed time after seems like a reasonable way to measure performance. On the JVM, it measures almost nothing useful. The first few thousand iterations run in the bytecode interpreter — 10-100x slower than compiled code. After JIT compilation kicks in, the JVM may eliminate your benchmark entirely through **dead code elimination** if it determines the result is never used. It might fold constant inputs through **constant folding**, turning your carefully crafted computation into a single precomputed value. And **on-stack replacement** during the loop creates a transition point that has no equivalent in real workloads.

**JMH** (Java Microbenchmark Harness) exists specifically because the JVM's optimizations make naive benchmarks unreliable. Written by the same engineers who build the JVM at Oracle, JMH handles warmup, prevents dead code elimination, runs benchmarks in isolated JVM processes, and reports results with statistical error margins. It is the only reliable way to microbenchmark Java code.

The fundamental insight is that JMH does not just time your code — it creates the conditions under which your code runs the way it would in production, after the JVM has fully optimized it.

sections.title: Setting Up JMH and Writing a Correct Benchmark
Warmup, Fork, and Blackhole: Defeating the JVM's Optimizations
sections.content:
Three JMH features directly counter JVM behaviors that corrupt naive benchmarks.

**`@Warmup(iterations = 5)`** lets the JIT compiler reach its stable optimization level before measurement begins. Without warmup, the first iterations run in the interpreter and the measurements include the compilation cost itself — numbers that are 10-100x slower than steady state. Five warmup iterations of 1 second each is enough for most code to reach C2-compiled performance.

**`@Fork(2)`** runs the benchmark in two separate JVM processes. This prevents **profile pollution** — where one benchmark's JIT optimizations leak into the next benchmark's measurements through shared profile data. Without forking, running benchmark A before benchmark B can change B's results because the JVM's profile-guided optimizations are influenced by A's execution patterns.

**`Blackhole.consume()`** is your defense against dead code elimination. When a benchmark computes a value that is never used — not returned, not stored, not passed to another method — the JVM is free to skip the computation entirely. Injecting a `Blackhole` and consuming the result forces the JVM to actually execute the code while adding negligible overhead to the measurement. This is especially important for benchmarks that compute intermediate values without producing a single final result.

sections.title: Reading JMH Output: When Error Margins Matter More Than Scores
sections.content:
JMH outputs results in either **Throughput** mode (operations per second) or **AverageTime** mode (nanoseconds per operation), along with error margins. Build and run the benchmark jar with Maven.

```bash
mvn package && java -jar target/benchmarks.jar
```

The error margin (reported as ±) is the most underrated number in the output. A result of `1,250,000 ±50,000 ops/s` is stable and trustworthy. A result of `1,250,000 ±500,000 ops/s` is meaningless — the variance is so high that the real throughput could be anywhere from 750K to 1.75M. High variance signals GC interference, CPU frequency scaling, or background processes contaminating the measurement.

For comparing two implementations, the error bars must not overlap. If implementation A is `1,200,000 ±100,000` and implementation B is `1,150,000 ±100,000`, the results overlap and you cannot claim A is faster. Run with more measurement iterations or reduce variance by pinning CPU frequency and closing background applications.

Never run JMH on shared CI runners with variable CPU frequency governors. Use dedicated bare-metal nodes or at minimum set the CPU governor to performance mode. Benchmark results on a throttled laptop running a video call are not results — they are noise with a confidence interval.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JMH prevents dead code elimination and JIT warmup errors** — naive loops are compiled away; JMH forces result consumption and runs warmup iterations before measurement; results are meaningful unlike `System.currentTimeMillis()` benchmarks
- **`@Benchmark` + `return result` or `Blackhole.consume(result)`** — return the result from the benchmark method; or inject `Blackhole` and call `blackhole.consume(result)`; either prevents the JIT from eliminating the computation
- **`@Warmup(iterations=5)` runs before measurement begins** — JIT-compiles the hot methods; measurement then reflects JIT-compiled performance, not interpreter performance; typically 5-10 warmup iterations are sufficient
- **Fork with `-f 1` for isolation** — each fork is a fresh JVM process; eliminates cross-benchmark JIT pollution; multiple forks average across JVM startup variations; the default 5 forks is thorough; 1 fork is quick for development
- **Only benchmark what flamegraphs identify as hot** — benchmarking a cold path produces an accurate number for something that doesn't matter; JMH results are only actionable when the benchmarked code is the measured bottleneck

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) exists because the JVM's JIT compiler and dead code elimination make naive benchmarks produce results that have nothing to do with actual performance. JMH handles these pitfalls automatically.

**Why naive benchmarks are wrong**
- The JVM optimizes away code that doesn't affect the program's output — a loop that computes a value but never uses it can be compiled to zero instructions; your "benchmark" measures nothing
- Dead code elimination: if the benchmarked code's result is never consumed, the JIT may eliminate the computation entirely; JMH requires returning the result from the benchmark method or using a `Blackhole` to consume it
- JIT warmup: the first executions of a method run in the interpreter; after enough invocations, the JIT compiles it; an early benchmark captures interpreter performance, not JIT-compiled performance; JMH runs multiple warmup iterations before recording measurements

**Writing a JMH benchmark**
- Annotate a class with `@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)`, `@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS)`, `@Warmup(iterations = 5)`, `@Measurement(iterations = 10)`
- Annotate the benchmark method with `@Benchmark`; return the result or pass it to `Blackhole.consume(result)` to prevent dead code elimination
- `@State(Scope.Benchmark)` on a class holding shared state ensures thread-safe state management across benchmark threads

**Running the benchmark**
- Build the benchmark JAR: `mvn clean verify`; run: `java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -f 1 -wi 5 -i 10`
- `-f 1`: one fork (new JVM process for isolation); `-wi 5`: 5 warmup iterations; `-i 10`: 10 measurement iterations; each iteration typically runs for 1 second
- Analyze the output: `ns/op` is nanoseconds per operation; `±` is the margin of error; results with high error margins indicate interference (GC, OS scheduling) — rerun with more forks

**What to benchmark**
- Benchmark the hot path that you measured as a bottleneck in production (flamegraph); benchmarking cold paths wastes time; JMH results are only meaningful for the specific JDK version, hardware, and configuration tested

sections.title: The Performance Tax You Do Not See Until Production Load Arrives
sections.content:
Spring Boot makes building applications fast. It also makes building slow applications easy. The framework's convention-over-configuration philosophy means that reasonable defaults handle most cases — but what is reasonable for development is not optimal for production. The gap shows up under load: endpoints that responded in 50ms during development take 500ms under 200 concurrent users.

These anti-patterns are not theoretical. They are the actual performance issues that surface in production Spring Boot services, and each one has the property of being invisible during development but painful under concurrency. An `ObjectMapper` created per request costs 2ms — unnoticeable in a unit test, devastating at 1000 requests per second. An N+1 query pattern adds 1 query per entity — invisible with 3 test records, catastrophic with 500.

The theme connecting all these anti-patterns is the same: **something expensive hiding behind something that looks cheap**. The method call looks innocent, the annotation looks declarative, the default looks reasonable. Under production load, the hidden cost multiplies by request volume and becomes the dominant performance factor.

sections.title: ObjectMapper Per Request: The 2ms Allocation Tax on Every Serialization
Hibernate N+1: The Silent Multiplier Behind Every 'Slow Database' Complaint
sections.content:
N+1 queries are the most common performance issue in Spring Boot applications using JPA. Hibernate defaults every `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` relationship to lazy loading, which sounds efficient until you access child entities in a loop. Loading 100 orders with their line items fires 101 queries: 1 for orders, 100 for line items.

Each individual query is fast enough to avoid slow query logs, making the problem invisible without Hibernate statistics. Enable detection with `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true` and watch the statement count per session.

Fix with **JOIN FETCH** in JPQL for explicit eager loading in specific queries, or set `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=16` as a global safety net. Batch fetching changes the N+1 into N/16+1 — still not ideal but a dramatic improvement that requires zero code changes.

The trap that catches teams is adding database indexes to fix what looks like a slow query problem. If the root cause is 100 fast queries, no index will help — you need to reduce the query count, not speed up individual queries. Always check the statement count before assuming the database is the bottleneck.

sections.title: Blocking on Reactive Threads, Eager Beans, and AOP Proxy Overhead
sections.content:
Three more anti-patterns surface in specific Spring Boot configurations.

**Blocking on reactive threads** affects services using WebFlux. Calling a blocking JDBC repository method on Netty's event-loop thread stalls not just that request but all requests sharing the thread. Netty uses a small number of event-loop threads (typically cores × 2), so blocking one thread on a 2-core container cuts throughput in half. The fix is either switching to **R2DBC** for reactive database access, offloading blocking work to `Schedulers.boundedElastic()`, or using Spring Boot 3.2+ with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`.

**Eager bean initialization** is the default in Spring Boot — all beans are created at startup. A large application with 500+ beans can take 10-15 seconds to start, burning container startup budget and slowing CI pipelines. Enable `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` to defer bean creation until first use. The trade-off is that misconfigured beans fail on first request instead of at startup, so mark critical infrastructure beans like DataSource and health checks with `@Lazy(false)` for fail-fast behavior.

**AOP proxy chains** add method-call indirection that is negligible for most beans but measurable on methods called thousands of times per second. A service method annotated with `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, and `@Timed` passes through three proxy layers on every call, adding 5-15 microseconds. Move annotations to the narrowest scope — `@Transactional` on the repository, not the service — and replace annotation-based metrics with manual `Micrometer` timer recording on truly hot paths.
